hints: Factorise the left-hand side $\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta$ as a difference of two squares.
Use the fundamental identity $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ and the double-angle identity $\cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$.
walkthrough:
Factorise the expression $\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta$ using the difference of two squares $A^2 - B^2 = (A - B)(A + B)$:
$$\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta = (\cos^2\theta)^2 - (\sin^2\theta)^2 = (\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta)(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)$$

Apply the double-angle formula for cosine $\cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$:
$$\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta \equiv \cos(2\theta)$$

hints: Express $4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta = (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)^2 = \sin^2(2\theta)$, then apply the double-angle formula $\sin^2(2\theta) = \dfrac{1 - \cos(4\theta)}{2}$.
Integrate term by term and evaluate between limits $-\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$.
walkthrough:
Simplify the integrand using part (a) and the double-angle formula for sine:
$$\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta = \cos(2\theta)$$
$$4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta = (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)^2 = \sin^2(2\theta)$$

Rewrite the full integrand in directly integrable form:
$$\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta + 4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta = \cos(2\theta) + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos(4\theta)$$

Integrate each term with respect to $\theta$:
$$\int \cos(2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta)$$
$$\int \dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\theta$$
$$\int -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(4\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -\dfrac{1}{8}\sin(4\theta)$$
Antiderivative:
$$F(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) + \dfrac{1}{2}\theta - \dfrac{1}{8}\sin(4\theta)$$

Subtract lower limit from upper limit:
$$F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) - F\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{16} - \dfrac{1}{8}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{16} + \dfrac{1}{8}\right)$$
$$= 2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{16} - \dfrac{1}{8}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}$$
